GSK's pharmaceutical sites were reactive to inspections by design. Each compliance risk lived in a different system — local SOPs checked manually against global requirements only when regulators arrived, trigger events going unlogged as formal deviations, and risk assessments sitting static while quality incidents accumulated. There was no aggregated view of inspection readiness across the network, and no way to act before an auditor walked in the door.

POC · 3 workstreams · Sterility Assurance scope · 2 sites
01 · QMS Alignment
Local SOPs were not continuously monitored against global QMS and regulatory requirements. Gaps were only discovered when auditors arrived — with no way to act proactively before an inspection.
02 · Missed Deviations
Trigger events — repeat alarms, out-of-spec results, non-routine maintenance — weren't consistently raising formal deviations. Potential compliance failures were falling through the cracks.
03 · GMP Risk Assessments
Sterility assurance risk assessments had unmonitored gaps against QMS requirements. No continuous improvement loop existed — learnings from deviations and quality events weren't feeding back in.
MVP · Expanded to 4–5 workstreams · 3 roles
04 · Investigation Quality
Deviation investigations lacked consistent rationale and classification. No visibility on AI overrule rates or investigation quality trends across the GSK network.
05 · Gemba & Oversight
No data-driven targeting for quality oversight on the shop floor across Production, Lab, Warehouse, and Utilities — leading to unforeseen regulatory observations and adverse quality trends.

The challenge wasn't just designing a tool — it was figuring out whether the data was even ready for one. The design process ran parallel to the data science discovery: every research finding changed the product scope, and every scoping decision changed the design.

Quality Oversight Specialist

Manual mapping is a major pain point. No standardised or automated way to link global SOP changes to local SOPs. Compliance processes are largely reactive. Teams benefit most from tools that highlight specific hotspots — not generic dashboards.

The discovery that changed everything

We set out to validate that data was ready to train an AI model. What we found: each site documented compliance differently — some in Excel, some in Word, some in legacy QMS systems. No consistent data pattern meant any model trained on the raw 11,000 gaps would produce unreliable results.

The pivot

We narrowed scope to Sterility Assurance — the one stream with mature, consistently structured data across sites. This was a research finding, not a product decision. The design constraint came from the data.

As-is process · mapped in the workshop with PMs + engineers

The broken link: Global QMS sends a change → QMS Champion manually identifies which local SOPs are affected → routes to SMEs → no system tracks whether it happened. Every step is manual, invisible to the global team, and prone to delay.

Three concepts explored · before we decided on the POC direction
CHOSEN
Concept 1 — Simpler, familiar
Task-based queue, builds on existing VI app structure. Lowest engineering lift for the POC. Users already operate in this pattern.
Concept 2 — Dashboard-first
Leads with an overview dashboard. Better for site leaders but higher cognitive load for daily reviewers. Deferred to MVP.
Concept 3 — Process-mapped flow
Closest to the existing QMS workflow. Complex interaction model with multiple branching paths. Too much re-training for a first version.
Why I advocated for Concept 1

Users already operate in task-based queues — QMS, ServiceNow, email inboxes. Concept 1 met them where they were, minimised re-training, and gave us the fastest path to validating the core feedback loop. That was the POC goal. Features from Concepts 2 and 3 were carried into the MVP.

Evaluation methodology · 4 stages · designed with the data science team

Parsing → Enrichment → Extraction → Gap Analysis. Each stage had a defined reviewer, platform, and feedback loop. I designed the Gap Analysis stage as the user-facing layer that fed directly back into model training.

Core design decisions

AI maps, human validates — every time

The AI maps each global requirement to the site's local procedure and flags gaps. But every AI finding is unconfirmed until a quality manager reviews it. The dashboard shows "AI says: Partial gap" — not "Partial gap" — until a human confirms.

Gap transparency — both documents, side by side

Every gap view shows the exact text of the global requirement next to the local procedure text. The AI highlights where the local text falls short. The reviewer can always see the source — nothing is hidden in a summary.

Corrections train the model

When a reviewer says the AI got it wrong, they pick the correct status and their reason is captured. The feedback form is part of the product, not a separate research channel. These corrections feed back into the training dataset.

Human-in-the-loop design

The AI surfaces 11,000 potential gaps. The quality manager's job is not to fix them — it's to validate which ones are real. The design separates those two jobs clearly: the AI does the searching, the human does the judging. A "Full gap" only becomes official when a person confirms it.

User journey — Quality Manager validating AI findings
1

Opens the task board

Sees all AI-flagged gaps for their site. Each row shows what the AI found — but nothing is confirmed yet. Filters by site, status, or searches by gap ID.

Confirms the AI is correct. Rates how close the section linkage was. Confirms the recommended action is right. All answers are captured for the training dataset.

Correction feeds back (when wrong)

If the AI was wrong — "this is No gap because we have a site-specific exemption" — the manager picks the correct status, selects the reason from a structured list, and that correction enters the training data.

Pharmaceutical manufacturing runs on legally-mandated quality investigations. When a batch fails an in-process check — a tablet weight reading falls outside limits, a lab result flags an anomaly — a full deviation investigation must follow. Root cause identified. Impact assessed. Corrective action proposed. Final report authored, reviewed, and signed — all to GxP standards, all traceable to a named, qualified person.

The science isn't what takes 3–6 months. The writing does. At GSK, investigators were manually switching between Veeva VQMS, the Lab Execution System (LES), SAP, and batch manufacturing records — none of them connected, none of them talking to each other. A scientist working a single deviation could spend entire days just copying readings from one system into another, reformatting observations into controlled document language, and re-drafting the same field every time new information arrived from the floor.

Beyond the time problem, there was a consistency problem. Investigations depended entirely on individual expertise. There was no structured way to surface similar historical deviations, no automatic check for whether a proposed corrective action conflicted with something already in the system, and no way to tell how past investigations had been classified or what CAPAs had closed them. Every investigation started from scratch. Every investigator made the same decisions in isolation.

The underlying tension was regulatory: GxP rules require that every entry in an investigation record is authored by a qualified person. AI could not simply write the record — that would break the audit trail that regulators and FDA inspectors rely on. But AI could draft, question, and surface evidence — if the interaction model kept authorship unambiguous at every step, in every field, all the way to write-back.

Co-design sessionsInteraction prototypingRegulatory alignmentExpert reviews

The design question that shaped everything: "Where to put the human, so that AI drafting is genuinely useful and every entry in the quality record stays attributable?" That question drove every interaction decision from the first prototype.

POC — Building the foundation

The POC established the core model: a 12-step investigation workspace, each step powered by a specialist AI agent. The agents don't complete forms. They draft proposals that arrive in a conversation panel alongside the editable record. The scientist reads each proposal, decides what to keep, and clicks Insert. The moment text lands in a field, it is marked "Agent draft, not yet reviewed" — flagged orange, explicitly not signed off. The moment the scientist edits that field — even one character — the label changes to "Reviewed by you." Green. Authored. The provenance has changed.

That provenance system was the foundation of the whole design. It solved the regulatory problem not through documentation but through the interaction model itself. The agent never puts anything on the record — the scientist always does. The final attestation page has no agent present at all. A dialog opens and lists exactly what will and won't happen — which fields, which record, which event — behind an explicit checkbox: "I confirm this investigation reflects my professional scientific judgment and I am the author of record." That checkbox is 21 CFR Part 11 and EU Annex 11 compliance by design.

The POC covered 12 investigation steps: 5W2H event description, Gemba observations recorded from the shop floor, human factor analysis (deliberately structured to avoid attribution to individuals), expected standard from controlled documents, gap analysis between standard and actual, repeat event search across historical records, impact and risk scoping for product and patient, direct cause identification backed by evidence, severity classification, simple investigation conclusion with CAPA decision, report summary, and write-back to the quality system.

MVP — Expanding to complex workflows

The MVP expanded the scope significantly. The dashboard added multi-event management — quality events could now contain multiple parallel investigations, each with its own state (open, in progress, closed) and a progress bar. The agent roster grew and deepened: a process map comparison step showing expected vs actual process flow side by side; a data variation analysis step with trend charts and control limit interpretation; a change assessment step checking recent change controls for connection to the event; and a full potential causes step using a fishbone diagram where the scientist could add, edit, or remove branches.

The 5-Why causal chain was one of the hardest design problems. The agent reasons to a root cause based on available evidence. But scientists often see it differently — they may know something the system doesn't, from a physical inspection or a floor conversation. The design had to allow branching at any node, keep both paths visible in the diagram without cluttering it, and maintain the audit trail throughout. The solution: a live SVG diagram that updated in real time as the chain was built or diverged. The active path was highlighted; the alternate path shown in a lighter state. Each node carried its evidence and the name of whoever confirmed or changed it.

The potential solutions step introduced an entirely new 3-stage workflow. Stage one: the agent generated 10+ solution options categorised by type — Eliminate, Prevent, Educate — each expandable with a full implementation plan and a deep-dive conversation. Stage two: a search of the historical CAPA and LTA database in Veeva, surfacing similar actions already in the system and flagging conflicts with actions already approved or in progress. Stage three: final selection with justification required for every solution not taken forward. That last requirement — written justification for rejected options — was not an auditing nicety. It was the difference between a CAPA package an FDA inspector could follow and one they would challenge.

The MVP also added an IRB (Investigation Review Board) workflow: preparing the board pack, recording the board's decision, and processing change requests that came back. The agent helped draft the executive summary and CAPA section, but the structure of the submission and the act of sending remained entirely with the scientist.

Core design decisions — the six principles that make it safe to use AI here

Drafting and recording are separate acts

AI drafts arrive with three buttons: Insert, Replace, Not useful. The agent cannot put anything into a field, save a step, or touch the quality record. Remove those three buttons and nothing moves.

Provenance is visible on every field

Text the agent wrote is marked "Agent draft, not yet reviewed" until the scientist edits it, when it becomes "Reviewed by you." The marker is about authorship, not correctness — the distinction an auditor cares about.

The agent declines

Ask it to classify the event, rate the risk, or save a step — it refuses and explains why. Where it is inferring rather than quoting, the draft says so. On the human factors step it will say the evidence is too thin rather than fill a field to be helpful.

Write-back is a deliberate act

The final page has no agent on it at all. It opens a dialog listing exactly what the action will and won't do, behind an explicit attestation. It touches one investigation record and nothing else.

Human-in-the-loop design

The AI never writes the final investigation report. It drafts hypotheses, surfaces similar past cases, runs the 5-Why chain, builds the fishbone — but every field is editable and every AI suggestion is labelled as a suggestion. The scientist's signature is the authoritative record. This keeps the product compliant with 21 CFR Part 11 and EU Annex 11.

30% ↑
CSAT improvement · Investigation timelines cut from 3–6 months to weeks

The POC went live as a pilot at one GSK site in late 2024. Investigation AI Release 1 launched in December 2025 with 50 scientists at pilot scale. The scale-up plan: 500+ users by February 2026, 5,000+ users across GSK's global pharmaceutical manufacturing sites by May 2026.

CSAT improved 30%. Investigation timelines, previously 3–6 months for a full deviation report, were cut to weeks. Scientists reported spending less time on administrative writing and more time on the scientific reasoning the investigation actually required. The structured workflow surfaced blockers earlier rather than letting them accumulate — where before an investigation might stall for weeks waiting for a document or a floor observation, the agent-driven step sequence made the gaps visible immediately.

The volume of open investigations at pilot sites dropped as the CAPA selection step — specifically the stage that surfaced conflicting or duplicate corrective actions already in the system — reduced rework loops. For the first time, investigators could see whether the action they were about to propose already existed, was already in progress, or actively contradicted something approved at the site level.

The potential benefit from extending the solution to Complaints investigations is estimated at £12.2 million per annum. The platform is now embedded in GSK's global quality deviation process and is a named milestone in their AI-in-quality roadmap — described by Simon Bamber (MSAT & Quality Data, Global Supply Chain Data & AI, GSK) as "the first step in our plan to proactively leverage AI in deviation investigations and a major step towards our ambition of Right First Time execution of quality processes."

The product was built to WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA — fully keyboard-operable, screen-reader compatible, and reflows correctly to 320px. In a regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing environment, an investigation workspace has to work for every scientist, including those with accessibility needs, on screens ranging from large lab monitors to tablets on the production floor.

FLOW's internal customer support tool — codenamed Inspector — was used daily by 6 teams: Customer Support, Deployments, CSM, Engineering, Product, and Accounts Reactivation. Despite this, it was never designed for any of them. All organisational data, impersonation workflows, production diagnostics, and admin actions were crammed into a single page of raw filter buttons — no hierarchy, no workflow structure, no feedback when actions were taken.

Support agents had developed their own workarounds just to do their jobs. When core workflows broke — impersonating a customer session, diagnosing a frozen org — the support operation stalled. And because Inspector was embedded in FLOW's monolith, it couldn't scale to single-tenant customers the business was beginning to onboard.

Inspector (before) — all sections on one page, every filter listed as a button, no data visible until clicked

Discovery Research · Sept 2022

12 participants · 6 teams · semi-structured interviews

The landing page was universally skipped

The blue filter buttons at the top — the most prominent UI — were the least-used features across every team. Agents went straight to Search instead, because the landing page surface showed no data.

Impersonation was distorting customer data

Inspector recorded impersonation as actual user logins. This meant support activity was showing up in customer engagement metrics, making it impossible to understand real customer behaviour at scale.

Finding an admin was a manual hunt

No clear admin indicator in Inspector. Support team members each had a different workaround: one checked the Integrations tab (whoever set it up is usually the admin), another went to Skills Inspector. CSMs saved admin links in OneNote.

No audit trail — zero accountability

There was no way to see when a user had been impersonated, what actions were taken, or who froze an org and why. This created compliance risk and made incident investigation slower for every team.

Key design decision from analysis

"Discard the existing model. Convert each category into its own screen — Org, User, Repo — with contextual filters for fast loading. The 'All' button on every section serves no one. Navigate to what you're looking for."

User Groups · Product Research

12 participants across 6 teams — grouped into support archetypes to anchor design decisions

Heuristic reviewUsability testingConcept validationJourney mapping

Four moves shaped the redesign from discovery through launch.

1

Research before wireframes

Ran 25 days of semi-structured interviews across all 6 teams. Mapped every use case, pain point, and workaround. Identified which features were used vs which were invisible. The research made the IA decision obvious: each category needed its own dedicated screen.

2

Retain everything, restructure the IA

No features were cut — the risk of agent re-learning was too high. Instead, restructured the information architecture around the actual support workflow: Org List → Org Detail (Info, Members, Integration, Feature Control, Repos, Reports) → User Actions. Added status columns, sortable tables, contextual search, and confirmation messages after every action.

3

Design for future scale

Pitched and built an architecture that could accommodate single-tenant customers — a new business direction at the time. Established 4 access roles (Read Only, Super User, Power User, CSM Prime) managed through Okta via ServiceNow. Each role had a clearly defined permission matrix — impersonation, feature flags, member management — built into the design.

4

Own the UAT

Proposed and authored the frontend UAT specification — a first for this team. Created structured test cases across 7 feature areas (Okta login, Org List, Org Detail, Members, Feature Control, Integrations, All Users), each with expected results and data conditions. This gave engineering a clear definition of "done" and eliminated the usual cycle of back-and-forth during release testing. All cases passed in prod on first execution.

Rumy Chatbot

Discovery researchStakeholder interviewsSession replay analysisJourney mapping

Games24x7 is one of India's largest real-money gaming platforms — Rummy and Fantasy products running at scale across millions of active players. At that scale, customer support becomes a product problem. Every gameplay confusion, every withdrawal query, every account issue generates a ticket. And when the platform had ~1.9 lakh tickets per month, all of them routed directly to human CS agents with no self-service layer, the system wasn't breaking — it had already broken.

Players had three separate places to look for help — Help, Contact Us, and Support — none of which led to the same place. "Help" on the web was marketing content. "Help" in the app was a list of FAQs. Neither was connected to anything that actually resolved the query. When a player raised an issue, they had no way to track it. If an FAQ article didn't answer their question, there was no clear path forward — they'd navigate back and forth trying to find a contact point, usually giving up before finding one.

The business goal was clear: get to 75% self-service resolution without human agent intervention. Only the genuinely complex 25% — disputes, edge cases, real-money escalations — should require a CS agent to open a ticket. Everything else should resolve in the chat.

Existing Help and Support touchpoints before redesign — three separate sections, inconsistent across web and app, no self-service path

Flow mappingPlatform evaluationConversational designUsability testing

The solution was to deploy a conversational AI — Rumy — as the first line of defense, powered by Haptik's conversational AI platform. But before any conversation was designed, the work started with mapping: where in the existing app would support touchpoints actually live, and what flows needed to be covered.

Step 1 — Map the existing app flow

I mapped the full existing app to identify every surface where a player might need help — game lobby, in-game, withdrawal, account, referral. This became the blueprint for where chatbot entry points would appear, ensuring support was accessible at the moment of need rather than hidden in a separate settings flow.

App flow map — proposed entry points for Help & Support across the product

Step 2 — Competitor research

I researched how comparable apps — Amazon, Zomato, Swiggy — handled conversational support, and looked closely at direct competitors: Junglee Rummy and Dream11. This established what players would already expect from an in-app chatbot, and what differentiated patterns were worth adopting.

Junglee Rummy — direct competitor

Dream11 — direct competitor

Step 3 — Design exploration

With the research done, I explored multiple design directions for every key component — 5 help home options, 2 chat initiation patterns, 3 CTA/page style variations — before converging on the final solution through stakeholder review.

Help Home — 5 design options explored before final direction selected

After months of research, ideation, and iteration — final designs were approved and handed off to engineering. The work covered the full support surface: a consolidated Help Home, a unified ticket creation flow, inner chat pages with feedback mechanisms, and before/after redesigns of the main menu and lobby screen.

5×
Install conversion — from 2% to 10.6% via redesigned register-before-download flow

Rumy launched as the single support entry point for Rummy and Fantasy, replacing the fragmented Help / Contact Us / Support setup entirely. The chatbot handled 40+ distinct conversation flows — gameplay rules, withdrawal queries, account issues, referral problems, live game support — without routing to a human agent. Response time dropped to under 10 seconds for the majority of queries. The CS team moved from handling every ticket to handling only the genuinely complex ones.

The register-before-download flow — a conversion redesign separate from the chatbot work — quintupled app install conversion from 2% to 10.6%. This was one of the highest-impact conversion improvements in the product's history. Removing the friction at the acquisition step, so that users registered their intent before being sent to the app store rather than after, was the core insight that drove the number.

The referral experience was rearchitected from a buried settings page into a shareable moment — a flow that felt native to the game rather than administrative. Referral-driven installs increased as a result. Across the full project — chatbot, conversion redesign, referral rework — this was a case where conversation design, information architecture, and acquisition flow design all ran in parallel toward the same business problem: a support and growth funnel that wasn't working at scale.

About

I really enjoy ambiguous problems. They usually excite me most. I don't need everything to come to me as a complete PRD with every requirement already figured out.

"I like getting into a problem when there are still many unknowns, exploring different possibilities, and figuring out what makes the most sense for that situation."

I am also a business-oriented person. I think about the business first: what value will this provide? If it provides value to the business, it should also create value for customers.

This is my approach. I keep this in mind when we create a product, enhance an existing one, or add something new. It should always create value for the business and stay user-focused, not technology-focused.
